Severe Flooding Disrupts Cyprus Construction Materials Industry, Supply Chains Strained

Heavy rainfall and severe flooding have brought significant disruption to Cyprus’s construction materials sector, with key production sites and transport routes across the southern and eastern regions still under water as of Thursday. The ongoing natural event has forced several quarries, cement plants, and aggregate depots to suspend operations, raising concerns over prolonged supply shortages and rising prices.

The floods, brought on by an unseasonably intense Mediterranean storm system, began late Monday and have since inundated areas surrounding Larnaca and Limassol, two major hubs for the island’s construction materials supply. According to the Cyprus Construction Materials Association, at least four major production sites along the Akrotiri salt flats and the outskirts of Larnaca have been forced to halt output due to waterlogged equipment and impassable access roads.

“Production has ground to a halt at our Larnaca facility,” said Andreas Petrou, operations director at Solidis Materials Ltd. “With main roads under water, we can neither bring in raw materials nor send out finished aggregates. The situation is critical.”

The flooding has also damaged secondary road networks, complicating the movement of heavy vehicles essential for transporting sand, gravel, cement, and concrete. The Ministry of Transport confirmed that sections of the A5 and B4 highways remain submerged, with emergency crews prioritizing the clearing of debris and pumping of water from strategic transport links.

Industry analysts warn that the disruption could trigger a spike in material prices and project delays if conditions persist. “Construction sites are already reporting shortages of key materials, and inventories are being depleted faster than expected,” observed Maria Xenou, senior analyst at CyFinance Advisory. “The industry is highly localized, so delays at these sites ripple quickly through the supply chain.”

The Cyprus Construction Workers Union has expressed concern for workers’ safety and job security, as temporary layoffs loom at shuttered plants. “Our members have been told to stay home for their own safety, but we are seeking government support to ensure wages are protected during this emergency,” said union president Stavros Ioannou.

Preliminary estimates from the Cyprus Construction Materials Association suggest that over 35% of the island’s total cement and aggregate production capacity is offline. While some inland facilities remain operational, they are struggling to meet surging demand from both contractors and local builders.

With the storm forecast to continue through the weekend, industry leaders are bracing for further disruptions. “We urge authorities to expedite drainage and road repairs,” said Petrou. “Every day of lost production sets back Cyprus’s construction sector by weeks.”

At press time, no timeline had been given for the resumption of normal operations, and the sector faces mounting uncertainty as floodwaters persist.
